chapters.title: Chapter 1: What the Forex Market Is

lessons.title: Who Trades Currencies and Why: Importers, Exporters, Banks, FPIs and the RBI

children.text: It is 9:00 am on a Monday and India's rupee market has just opened. In Mumbai, an oil company's treasury desk needs dollars to pay for a crude cargo. In Bengaluru, an IT company wants to convert last month's US billings into rupees. In Singapore, a foreign fund is selling Indian shares and wants its money out in dollars. In Kerala, thousands of families are receiving money sent from the Gulf. And at the RBI, someone is watching all of it. Every one of these players is on the USD/INR screen for a different reason. This lesson shows you who they are, which way each one pushes the rupee, and why that matters more than any chart pattern.

body.text: The rupee's price is a tug of war between people who need dollars and people who have dollars to sell. Know who is pulling on each side, and exchange rate moves stop looking random.

children.text: Two Sides of the Rope

Forget currency jargon for a moment and think of USD/INR as the price of a dollar. Anyone who must pay someone abroad needs to buy dollars, which pushes the price of a dollar up and the rupee down. Anyone who has earned or received dollars and needs rupees must sell dollars, which pushes the rupee up. Every participant in this lesson falls on one side or the other, sometimes both.

body.title: Who weakens the rupee vs who strengthens it

columns.label: Buy dollars, sell rupees (rupee weakens)
points: Importers paying for crude oil, gold, electronics and machinery
FPIs selling Indian shares or bonds and taking money home
Indians paying foreign tuition, travel or investing abroad under LRS
RBI when it buys dollars to build reserves

columns.label: Sell dollars, buy rupees (rupee strengthens)
points: Exporters of goods, such as pharma, textiles and engineering firms
IT and services companies converting overseas revenue
NRIs and Indians working abroad sending money home
FPIs and foreign companies investing in India
RBI when it sells dollars from reserves to support the rupee

children.text: Importers and Exporters: The Real Economy

Trade is the foundation of currency demand. India imports far more physical goods than it exports, led by crude oil, gold and electronics. That gap creates a steady, structural need for dollars. India's saving grace is services: software, consulting and back-office work sold abroad bring in a huge flow of dollars, and so do remittances from Indians working overseas.

stats.label: Merchandise trade deficit
stats.context: FY26, goods imported minus goods exported

stats.label: Net private transfers
stats.context: FY26, mainly remittances from Indians abroad

body.title: Find the import bill
body.prompt: In FY26, India's merchandise exports were $441.78 billion and the merchandise trade deficit was $333.20 billion. What were India's merchandise imports, in $ billion?
body.explanation: Trade deficit = imports minus exports, so imports = exports + deficit = $441.78 billion + $333.20 billion = $774.98 billion. For every $100 of goods India sold abroad, it bought roughly $175 worth. Every one of those import dollars had to be bought in the forex market.

body.title: India's Goods and Services Trade, FY26 ($ billion)

children.text: Read the chart as a flow of dollars. Goods pull about $333 billion out of India. Services put about $214 billion back. Remittances add roughly another $145 billion. That is why Indian IT companies and Gulf workers matter to the rupee just as much as Indian Oil and gold jewellers do.

body.text: Importers and exporters behave differently when the rupee moves. When the rupee is falling, importers rush to buy dollars before it gets worse, while exporters hold back their dollars hoping for a better rate. Both actions push the rupee down further. This is why currency moves often feed on themselves in the short run.

children.text: Banks: The Market Makers in the Middle

markDefs.definition: A bank licensed by RBI under FEMA to deal in foreign exchange with customers and other banks. Most large Indian and foreign banks in India hold this licence.
The gap between the price at which a dealer buys a currency and the price at which it sells. This is how banks earn on customer forex deals.

children.text: An oil company does not ring up a Tiruppur exporter to swap dollars. Both deal with banks. In India, only an
Authorised Dealer bank
such as SBI, HDFC Bank or ICICI Bank can buy and sell foreign currency with customers. Banks quote a buy price and a sell price, earn the
spread
in between, and pass leftover positions to other banks in the interbank market. Banks also trade on their own account, taking views on where the rupee is headed.

body.caption: Who is on the other side of global forex trades, April 2025 (BIS Triennial Survey)

cells: Dealer banks trading with each other
Other financial institutions (smaller banks, institutional investors, hedge funds, official sector)
Non-financial customers (companies that import, export or invest)

body.text: Only about 5% of global forex turnover involves non-financial companies, the importers and exporters who actually need foreign currency. Shares add to 101% because of rounding. The other 95% or so is banks, funds and financial firms trading with each other. Trade flows set the long-term direction of a currency, but day to day, finance does most of the pushing.

children.text: FPIs: The Fastest Money in the Room

markDefs.definition: Foreign Portfolio Investors. Overseas funds and institutions registered with SEBI that buy listed Indian shares, bonds and other securities.

children.text: When a US pension fund buys Infosys shares on NSE, it first has to convert dollars into rupees. When it sells and leaves, it converts rupees back into dollars. Multiply that across thousands of funds and you get the single most volatile force on the rupee.
FPIs

can move billions of dollars in or out of India within weeks, and they react to things outside India: US bond yields, crude oil prices, a stronger dollar, or a better opportunity in another emerging market.

body.label: FPI net selling of Indian equities in 2026 (till 11 September)
body.context: Already more than the ₹1.66 lakh crore FPIs withdrew in the whole of 2025, per NSDL data. Rising US yields and Brent crude above $100 were cited as key triggers.

body.caption: How much dollar demand an FPI exit creates

body.title: Two weeks of FPI selling
body.prompt: FPIs pulled ₹13,138 crore out of Indian equities in the first two weeks of September 2026. If they converted all of it into dollars at USD/INR 95.50, roughly how many million dollars would they have bought? Round to the nearest million.
body.explanation: ₹13,138 crore = ₹1,31,38,00,00,000, or 131.38 billion rupees. Divide by 95.50: 131.38 ÷ 95.50 = 1.3757 billion, about $1,376 million. That is more than $1.3 billion of extra dollar demand in two weeks, from one group of participants.

children.text: The RBI: The Referee Who Also Plays

markDefs.definition: The stock of foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and IMF reserve position held by RBI, used to pay for imports in a crisis and to smooth currency moves.

children.text: The RBI writes the rules for India's forex market under FEMA, but it is also a participant. It does not try to make a profit and says it does not target any specific level for the rupee. Its stated aim is to curb excessive volatility. When dollars flood in, it buys them and adds to its
forex reserves

, which stops the rupee from rising too fast. When dollars rush out, it sells from those reserves to slow the rupee's fall. It cannot stop a trend driven by oil and FPI flows, but it can take the panic out of it.

body.label: India's forex reserves, week ended 4 September 2026
body.context: A record high, per RBI weekly data, making India the fourth-largest reserve holder in the world after China, Japan and Switzerland.

body.title: How RBI actually steps into the market

children.text: Spot market.
RBI buys or sells dollars for immediate delivery, usually through public sector banks. Dealers often spot this as state-run banks suddenly selling dollars near a key level.
Forward market.
RBI takes positions for future dates, which lets it act without spending reserves today.
Offshore NDF market.
Pressure on the rupee often builds in offshore non-deliverable forwards before Indian markets open. You will learn how this market works in the next lesson.
Policy measures.
RBI can also change the flow itself, for example by making it more attractive for NRIs to park foreign currency deposits in India, as it did with its June 2026 measures.
Speculators and Retail Traders: The Smallest Players

Hedge funds, proprietary trading firms and individual traders trade currencies purely to profit from price moves. Globally, hedge funds and prop firms account for about 8% of turnover. Retail traders are a sliver of that. If you trade USD/INR futures on NSE from your Zerodha account, you are not moving the rupee. You are reacting to the importers, exporters, FPIs and RBI who do. That is the most useful mindset a retail currency trader can have.

Invest in or exit Indian securities
Foreign funds buying or selling Nifty stocks

body.title: Who strengthens the rupee?
body.question: Which of these transactions pushes the rupee stronger against the dollar?
options: Indian Oil paying a Saudi supplier for a crude cargo
A foreign fund selling ₹2,000 crore of HDFC Bank shares and repatriating the money
Infosys converting $300 million of US revenue into rupees
A Delhi family paying a US university's tuition fees
body.explanation: Infosys is selling dollars and buying rupees, which adds rupee demand. The other three all need to buy dollars: an importer paying a supplier, an FPI leaving India, and a family paying overseas fees.

body.title: Read the rupee's day
body.scenario: On a Tuesday, Brent crude jumps 4% to $110 a barrel after a Middle East flare-up. Overnight, US 10-year bond yields rise sharply. By noon, NSDL data shows FPIs sold a large block of Indian shares the previous day. Meanwhile, a large Indian IT company announces a multi-year deal with a European bank. USD/INR opens at 95.50 and moves to 96.10 by 11:00 am, then suddenly stalls as dealers report state-run banks selling dollars.
body.prompt: Identify each participant in this scenario, say which way each one pushes the rupee, and explain what most likely caused the stall at 96.10.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Importers, especially oil marketing companies, need more dollars for the same crude volume when Brent jumps. This weakens the rupee.
2. FPIs selling Indian shares, partly because higher US yields make US bonds more attractive, need to buy dollars to exit. This also weakens the rupee.
3. The IT deal is positive for future dollar inflows, but those dollars arrive over months and years, so it does little on the day.
4. Importers may also rush to buy dollars as the rupee falls, and exporters may hold back, adding to the move.
5. State-run banks suddenly selling dollars near a round level is the classic sign of RBI intervention. RBI is not trying to reverse the trend, only to stop a disorderly slide, so the rupee stalls rather than rebounding sharply.

body.title: Your five-minute morning check on the rupee
steps: Check Brent crude. A sharp rise means more dollar demand from importers.
Check the US Dollar Index. A stronger dollar globally usually drags the rupee down too.
Check US 10-year bond yields. Rising yields tend to pull FPI money out of emerging markets.
Check the previous day's FPI flows on NSDL's FPI Monitor.
Check the offshore NDF quote or pre-open USD/INR level for how the rupee is likely to open.

body.label: NSDL FPI Monitor
body.description: Official FPI net investment data for Indian equities, debt and other segments. Watch this to understand one of the biggest forces on the rupee.

body.title: The referee's goal
body.textWithBlank: RBI says it does not target a specific level for the rupee. It intervenes to curb excessive ___.
body.explanation: RBI's stated aim is to smooth disorderly moves, not to defend a fixed exchange rate. That is why it slows a falling rupee rather than pushing it back to an old level.

cards.definition: A bank licensed by RBI under FEMA to deal in foreign exchange with customers and other banks.
The gap between a dealer's buying and selling price for a currency. It is how banks earn on customer forex deals.
Foreign Portfolio Investor. An overseas fund registered with SEBI to invest in listed Indian securities.
The amount by which goods imports exceed goods exports. For India, $333.20 billion in FY26.
Foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and IMF reserve position held by RBI to smooth currency moves and meet external payments.
RBI buying or selling dollars, usually through state-run banks, to curb excessive volatility in the rupee.

points: USD/INR is set by a tug of war between those who must buy dollars and those who have dollars to sell.
Importers, FPIs leaving India and Indians spending abroad weaken the rupee. Exporters, IT companies, remittances and incoming investment strengthen it.
India's large goods trade deficit, $333.20 billion in FY26, is partly offset by services exports and record remittances.
Banks sit in the middle as market makers, and globally financial institutions account for about 95% of forex turnover.
FPIs are the fastest-moving force on the rupee. They sold ₹2.37 lakh crore of Indian equities in 2026 till 11 September.
RBI is both rule-maker and participant. It uses its reserves to curb excessive volatility, not to fix a level.
Retail traders do not move the rupee. They react to the players who do.
